ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was granted ethical approval from the University of Leeds Ethics Committee (BESS + FREC 2023 -0792 -877).

Based on the results obtained from an a priori G*Power analysis (Faul et al., 2007), at least 36 participants were required to achieve a well-powered study (1 -β = 0.95), with a medium effect size (f = 0.25), and significant alpha criterion (α = .05) for individuals who completed four experimental manipulations (2 x 2 within-participants design).
table.formatted: Based on the results obtained from an a priori G*Power analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Faul et al., 2007)</ref>, at least 36 participants were required to achieve a well-powered study (1 -β = 0.95), with a medium effect size (f = 0.25), and significant alpha criterion (α = .05) for individuals who completed four experimental manipulations (2 x 2 within-participants design).

table.text: Therefore, forty-eight participants were recruited to achieve a fully counterbalanced order of experimental conditions.
Participants were recruited via a convenience sampling method from the University of Leeds Driving Simulator database.
However, eye tracking data from 4 participants were not recorded due to failure at the calibration stage.

Participants provided informed consent prior to taking part in the experiment (both in verbal and written format, i.e., signing a consent form), and strict protocol was in place to make sure standardised instructions were provided to all participants.
Participants completed four experimental drives, presented in a counterbalanced order, with a 5-minute break after every two drives.

For the manual driving conditions, participants were told that they had full control of the movement of the car, and they were instructed to follow the traffic rules as they would when they were driving in a real urban setting with a speed limit of 30 mph.
During these conditions, participants were first exposed to one minute of manual driving before the system became available.

When the system first became available, an auditory message "Automation Available" was presented, and participants were instructed to engage with the system as soon as possible by pressing a specified button on the steering wheel.

For this reason, participants were required to monitor the road environment at all times and take over manual control if necessary by pressing the specified buttons on the steering wheel or turning the steering wheel for more than 2 degrees or pressing the brake pedal.
Upon arrival, participants were briefed on the experimental procedure and allowed to ask any questions they might have regarding the experiment before providing their consent.

Participants completed a series of self-report measures to provide their trust and perceived safety towards automated vehicles prior to the experimental drives (data are not reported in this manuscript).
Participants were accompanied by the experimenter during these drives.
Participants completed four experimental drives on their own, each of which lasted approximately 9 minutes.

Once all experimental drives were completed, participants were once again asked to complete a series of self-report measures to report their perceived driving skills, difficulties associated with driving after dark and their trust and perceived safety towards automated vehicles (data are not reported in this manuscript).
Participants were then debriefed and compensated £30 for their time.

Also, for practical reasons, participants took part in this driving simulator study during daytime hours, which limits our understanding of how circadian rhythms may have affected driver fatigue and influenced performance.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Based on the results obtained from an a priori G*Power analysis (Faul et al., 2007), at least 36 participants were required to achieve a well-powered study (1 -β = 0.95), with a medium effect size (f = 0.25), and significant alpha criterion (α = .05) for individuals who completed four experimental manipulations (2 x 2 within-participants design). Therefore, forty-eight participants were recruited to achieve a fully counterbalanced order of experimental conditions. Participants were recruited via a convenience sampling method from the University of Leeds Driving Simulator database. However, eye tracking data from 4 participants were not recorded due to failure at the calibration stage. Data from 44 participants (20 female, 24 male) was used for the analysis. Participants ranged in age from 25 to 63 years old (M = 40.23; SD = 11.19) and held a valid UK driving license for at least 3 years (M = 19.30; SD = 12.24). Their annual mileage ranged from 3000 to 18000 miles (M = 8125; SD = 3313), and they had normal or corrected-to-normal vision. The study was granted ethical approval from the University of Leeds Ethics Committee (BESS + FREC 2023 -0792 -877). Participants provided informed consent prior to taking part in the experiment (both in verbal and written format, i.e., signing a consent form), and strict protocol was in place to make sure standardised instructions were provided to all participants. Data collection period spanned between 30 October 2023 to 23 November 2023.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .126", "p =.533", "p = .562", "p =.704", "p > .05", "p > .05", "p = 1.000"), Sentence = c("The main effect of level of automation on horizontal gaze dispersion was not found to be significant (F (1, 115.39) = 2.380, p = .126).", "Both horizontal (F (1, 114.92) = 0.391, p =.533) and vertical gaze dispersion (F (1, 118.24) = 0.339, p = .562) were found to be similar across daytime and after dark driving environments.", "Both horizontal (F (1, 114.92) = 0.391, p =.533) and vertical gaze dispersion (F (1, 118.24) = 0.339, p = .562) were found to be similar across daytime and after dark driving environments.", "No significant interactions were found for horizontal gaze dispersion (F (1, 114.92) = 0.145, p =.704).", "Based on the model prediction, participants reduced their glance time towards the forward roadway area in L2 assisted driving No significant main effect of lighting conditions was found for the percentage of glance time towards any of the four AOIs (p > .05).", "There was also no significant interaction effect across the four experimental conditions for the percentage of glance time towards any of the four AOIs (p > .05).", "Post-hoc Bonferronicorrected comparisons showed that the BP elements elicited significantly longer mean glance durations than IO, only during daytime conditions (z = 3.39, p = .004), with no significant differences found after dark (p = 1.000)." )), row.names = c(NA, -7L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 153 columns across 5 data files.
#### Issues Identified
6 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("SUMMARY OF GLANCE.xlsx", "SUMMARY OF GLANCE.xlsx", "SUMMARY OF GLANCE.xlsx", "SUMMARY OF GLANCE.xlsx", "SUMMARY OF GLANCE.xlsx", "SUMMARY OF GLANCE.xlsx"), Column = c("No Of Glances - Left Group of Talking Pedestrians - Instrument Cluster", "No Of Glances - Left Group of Talking Pedestrians - Left Periphery", "No Of Glances - Left Group of Talking Pedestrians - Right Periphery", "No Of Glances - Right Group of Talking Pedestrians - Instrument Cluster", "No Of Glances - Right Group of Talking Pedestrians - Left Periphery", "No Of Glances - Right Group of Talking Pedestrians - Right Periphery" ), Issues = c("🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has a length of 70 characters (SPSS allows at most 64, ...", "🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has a length of 66 characters (SPSS allows at most 64, ...", "🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has a length of 67 characters (SPSS allows at most 64, ...", "🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has a length of 71 characters (SPSS allows at most 64, ...", "🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has a length of 67 characters (SPSS allows at most 64, ...", "🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has a length of 68 characters (SPSS allows at most 64, ..." )), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 5 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: The study was granted ethical approval from the University of Leeds Ethics Committee (BESS + FREC 2023 -0792 -877).
live_data_statements: Based on the results obtained from an a priori G*Power analysis (Faul et al., 2007), at least 36 participants were required to achieve a well-powered study (1 -β = 0.95), with a medium effect size (f = 0.25), and significant alpha criterion (α = .05) for individuals who completed four experimental manipulations (2 x 2 within-participants design).
Therefore, forty-eight participants were recruited to achieve a fully counterbalanced order of experimental conditions.
Participants were recruited via a convenience sampling method from the University of Leeds Driving Simulator database.
However, eye tracking data from 4 participants were not recorded due to failure at the calibration stage.

Participants provided informed consent prior to taking part in the experiment (both in verbal and written format, i.e., signing a consent form), and strict protocol was in place to make sure standardised instructions were provided to all participants.
Participants completed four experimental drives, presented in a counterbalanced order, with a 5-minute break after every two drives.

For the manual driving conditions, participants were told that they had full control of the movement of the car, and they were instructed to follow the traffic rules as they would when they were driving in a real urban setting with a speed limit of 30 mph.
During these conditions, participants were first exposed to one minute of manual driving before the system became available.

When the system first became available, an auditory message "Automation Available" was presented, and participants were instructed to engage with the system as soon as possible by pressing a specified button on the steering wheel.

For this reason, participants were required to monitor the road environment at all times and take over manual control if necessary by pressing the specified buttons on the steering wheel or turning the steering wheel for more than 2 degrees or pressing the brake pedal.
Upon arrival, participants were briefed on the experimental procedure and allowed to ask any questions they might have regarding the experiment before providing their consent.

Participants completed a series of self-report measures to provide their trust and perceived safety towards automated vehicles prior to the experimental drives (data are not reported in this manuscript).
Participants were accompanied by the experimenter during these drives.
Participants completed four experimental drives on their own, each of which lasted approximately 9 minutes.

Once all experimental drives were completed, participants were once again asked to complete a series of self-report measures to report their perceived driving skills, difficulties associated with driving after dark and their trust and perceived safety towards automated vehicles (data are not reported in this manuscript).
Participants were then debriefed and compensated £30 for their time.

Also, for practical reasons, participants took part in this driving simulator study during daytime hours, which limits our understanding of how circadian rhythms may have affected driver fatigue and influenced performance.

text.text: Driving Simulator Team at the University of Leeds for their dedication in creating the simulated driving environments.
In addition, the authors would also like to thank Tobii for the use of the Tobii Glasses 3 for collecting the eye tracking data in the present study.
Part of the findings of the present study will be presented at the 10 th International Conference on Driver Distraction and Inattention (DDI2026) at Gothenburg, Sweden.
Vehicles equipped with assisted driving technologies such as SAE L2 (SAE, 2021) are now available to many consumers.
text.formatted: Vehicles equipped with assisted driving technologies such as SAE L2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(SAE, 2021)</ref> are now available to many consumers.

text.text: These technologies provide support to drivers for both lateral and longitudinal movement of the vehicle.
When L2 driving assistance is engaged, drivers are no longer involved in the moment-to-moment physical control of the vehicle.

However, they are required to stay engaged in the driving task, by monitoring both the road environment and the assistance systems, to identify any potential system limitations (SAE, 2021), intervening if they identify a situation that cannot be handled by the system and could lead to a collision.
text.formatted: However, they are required to stay engaged in the driving task, by monitoring both the road environment and the assistance systems, to identify any potential system limitations <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(SAE, 2021)</ref>, intervening if they identify a situation that cannot be handled by the system and could lead to a collision.

text.text: Previous studies have shown that drivers spend less time monitoring the forward roadway during L2 assisted driving, resulting a lower percentage of glance time towards road centre and increased visual attention towards areas away from the road centre (Gaspar & Carney, 2019; Pipkorn et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Previous studies have shown that drivers spend less time monitoring the forward roadway during L2 assisted driving, resulting a lower percentage of glance time towards road centre and increased visual attention towards areas away from the road centre <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Gaspar & Carney, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Pipkorn et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This shift of visual attention may occur as drivers are no longer involved in the moment-to-moment control of the vehicle, thereby reducing the need for continuous monitoring of the forward roadway.

In addition, when hands-off L2 is engaged, drivers show more extensive horizontal scanning of the driving environment (Louw & Merat, 2017), which may be advantageous for hazard detection (Mackenzie & Harris, 2015).
text.formatted: In addition, when hands-off L2 is engaged, drivers show more extensive horizontal scanning of the driving environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Louw & Merat, 2017)</ref>, which may be advantageous for hazard detection <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Mackenzie & Harris, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Assisted driving has also been shown to alter drivers' vertical gaze patterns.

During uninterrupted motorway driving, Goncalves et al. (2020) found lower vertical gaze dispersion when L2 assisted driving was operational compared with manual driving, while Louw & Merat (2017) observed a similar pattern following an initial familiarisation period with the driving environment and the automated system.
text.formatted: During uninterrupted motorway driving, <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Goncalves et al. (2020)</ref> found lower vertical gaze dispersion when L2 assisted driving was operational compared with manual driving, while <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Louw & Merat (2017)</ref> observed a similar pattern following an initial familiarisation period with the driving environment and the automated system.

text.text: Drivers have also been found to devote less attention towards the dashboard area during uninterrupted urban driving under hands-off L2 assisted driving (Qin et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Drivers have also been found to devote less attention towards the dashboard area during uninterrupted urban driving under hands-off L2 assisted driving <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Qin et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, the opposite pattern has been observed during transitions of control.

During transitions of control, drivers require information both from the forward roadway and instrument cluster to acquire information about the disengagement of the driving assistance system, resulting in significantly higher vertical gaze dispersion when compared to manual driving condition (Goncalves et al., 2020).
text.formatted: During transitions of control, drivers require information both from the forward roadway and instrument cluster to acquire information about the disengagement of the driving assistance system, resulting in significantly higher vertical gaze dispersion when compared to manual driving condition <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Goncalves et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: While the aforementioned studies establish how the presence of L2 assisted driving alters gaze patterns, most evidence are primarily based on results from motorway settings and car-following scenarios (Louw & Merat, 2017; Morando et al., 2019; Morando et al., 2020; Morando et al., 2021; Pipkorn et al., 2024; Pipkorn et al., 2025), with relatively little focus on urban driving environment.
text.formatted: While the aforementioned studies establish how the presence of L2 assisted driving alters gaze patterns, most evidence are primarily based on results from motorway settings and car-following scenarios <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Louw & Merat, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Morando et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Morando et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Morando et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Pipkorn et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Pipkorn et al., 2025)</ref>, with relatively little focus on urban driving environment.

text.text: Whether these insights could be extended to busy urban environment remains underexplored.

Urban environments have a higher prevalence of peripheral hazards, including the presence of pedestrians and cyclists. Underwood et al. (2002) found that participants who watched video recordings of suburban scenes from a driver's point of view exhibited a greater dispersion of horizontal fixations, compared to motorway scenes.
text.formatted: Urban environments have a higher prevalence of peripheral hazards, including the presence of pedestrians and cyclists. <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Underwood et al. (2002)</ref> found that participants who watched video recordings of suburban scenes from a driver's point of view exhibited a greater dispersion of horizontal fixations, compared to motorway scenes.

text.text: Critically, the increased visual demand in an urban environment requires drivers to actively search for potential hazards, failure in doing so may delay hazard detection, resulting in a potential collision.
The reduction in operational demands when L2 assisted driving is operational may facilitate such visual searching behaviours by freeing attentional resources for monitoring the driving environment.
However, it remains unclear how visual attention is being reallocated during L2 assisted driving in complex urban environments.
Based on the STATS 19 database, driving after dark is associated with a higher percentage of road traffic collisions (RTC) (Fotios et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Based on the STATS 19 database, driving after dark is associated with a higher percentage of road traffic collisions (RTC) <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Fotios et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: One of the potential factors contributing to this heightened risk is the inherent difficulty in perceiving the driving environment in low visibility (Wood, 2020).
text.formatted: One of the potential factors contributing to this heightened risk is the inherent difficulty in perceiving the driving environment in low visibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Wood, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This degradation can potentially increase drivers' reaction time for detecting hazards by up to 400ms, compared to optimal daytime conditions (Plainis & Murray, 2002).
text.formatted: This degradation can potentially increase drivers' reaction time for detecting hazards by up to 400ms, compared to optimal daytime conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Plainis & Murray, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: As drivers are allowed to engage L2 assisted driving systems after dark (Gershon et al., 2023), it is currently unclear how this would influence their visual scanning patterns and attention allocation across different Areas of Interest (AOIs) when the system is engaged.
text.formatted: As drivers are allowed to engage L2 assisted driving systems after dark <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Gershon et al., 2023)</ref>, it is currently unclear how this would influence their visual scanning patterns and attention allocation across different Areas of Interest (AOIs) when the system is engaged.

text.text: Results from manual driving studies show that drivers adapt their visual scanning behaviour due to the visual challenges encountered after dark.
Specifically, reduced visual acuity after dark may reduce bottom-up modulations of visual attention, as environmental stimuli become less salient.

Consequently, drivers often exhibit a restricted distribution of fixations across the driving environment (Gruner & Ansorge, 2017) and are less likely to engage in mirror-checking behaviours (Urwyler et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Consequently, drivers often exhibit a restricted distribution of fixations across the driving environment <ref type="bibr">(Gruner & Ansorge, 2017)</ref> and are less likely to engage in mirror-checking behaviours <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Urwyler et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: To compensate for this lack of visual acuity, drivers require a longer time to process visual inputs, once they are detected, leading to significantly longer fixation durations, compared to daytime conditions (Konstantopoulos et al., 2010; Urwyler et al., 2015).
text.formatted: To compensate for this lack of visual acuity, drivers require a longer time to process visual inputs, once they are detected, leading to significantly longer fixation durations, compared to daytime conditions <ref type="bibr">(Konstantopoulos et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Urwyler et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: However, it is currently unclear how these visual scanning adaptations to reduced visibility in after dark driving conditions interact with the attentional reallocation associated with L2 assisted driving.

Given that L2 assisted driving reduces drivers' operational demands from moment-to-moment basis, it may free attentional resources that could compensate for the increased attentional demands associated with reduced visibility in after dark driving environment.

A further consideration is that hazards in an urban environment take a variety of forms, with previous research suggesting that drivers may be more attracted to certain hazard types over others (Crundall et al., 2012).
text.formatted: A further consideration is that hazards in an urban environment take a variety of forms, with previous research suggesting that drivers may be more attracted to certain hazard types over others <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Crundall et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, Crundall et al. (2012) introduced the distinction between Behavioural Prediction (BP) and Environmental Prediction (EP) events.
text.formatted: Specifically, <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Crundall et al. (2012)</ref> introduced the distinction between Behavioural Prediction (BP) and Environmental Prediction (EP) events.

text.text: BP events involve road users whose actions can be directly observed and anticipated, such as a pedestrian visible at the roadside and walking towards the roadway.

In contrast, EP events involve an object that obscures a driver's view of the surrounding environment (e.g., a parked vehicle), and drivers have to infer the probability of a hidden hazard emerging from it.

It is argued that BP stimuli attract more attention compared to EP stimuli, because BP stimuli are directly observable, dynamic, entities that are more likely to trigger bottom-up attentional mechanisms.

Given that urban environments contain a variety of BP and EP elements, it remains unclear whether attention allocation towards these different types of ambient traffic varies across lighting conditions and levels of automation.

In light of the aforementioned research gaps, the present study explored drivers' visual attention allocation and scanning patterns, comparing manual driving and hands-off L2 assisted driving during uninterrupted driving in daytime and after dark conditions in an urban setting and explored whether different types of ambient traffic would trigger different attention allocation patterns across experimental conditions.
The following research questions were proposed: 1.

How does drivers' visual attention allocation and scanning patterns differ between the two levels of driving (manual and assisted driving) and lighting conditions of the driving environment (daytime and after dark)?
How does drivers' visual attention allocation towards different element types differ across experimental conditions?

text.text: Based on the results obtained from an a priori G*Power analysis (Faul et al., 2007), at least 36 participants were required to achieve a well-powered study (1 -β = 0.95), with a medium effect size (f = 0.25), and significant alpha criterion (α = .05) for individuals who completed four experimental manipulations (2 x 2 within-participants design).

text.text: Therefore, forty-eight participants were recruited to achieve a fully counterbalanced order of experimental conditions.
Participants were recruited via a convenience sampling method from the University of Leeds Driving Simulator database.
However, eye tracking data from 4 participants were not recorded due to failure at the calibration stage.
Data from 44 participants (20 female, 24 male) was used for the analysis.
Participants ranged in age from 25 to 63 years old (M = 40.23; SD = 11.19) and held a valid UK driving license for at least 3 years (M = 19.30; SD = 12.24).
Their annual mileage ranged from 3000 to 18000 miles (M = 8125; SD = 3313), and they had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
The study was granted ethical approval from the University of Leeds Ethics Committee (BESS + FREC 2023 -0792 -877).

Participants provided informed consent prior to taking part in the experiment (both in verbal and written format, i.e., signing a consent form), and strict protocol was in place to make sure standardised instructions were provided to all participants.
Data collection period spanned between 30 October 2023 to 23 November 2023.
The study was conducted in a high-fidelity motion-based driving simulator -the second-generation University of Leeds Driving Simulator (UoLDS; see Figure 1).
text.formatted: The study was conducted in a high-fidelity motion-based driving simulator -the second-generation University of Leeds Driving Simulator (UoLDS; see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: This included a Jaguar S-Type car, placed within a 4-metre spherical dome, with an operational steering wheel and pedals, providing a safe, highly immersive and controlled environment to analyse drivers' behaviour.
Projectors equipped within the dome provided a 300-degree projection which displayed the driving environment.
The head-mounted Tobii Pro Glasses 3 (Tobii AB, 2024) were used to collect gaze data.
This eye tracker collects gaze data at a 50 Hz sampling rate with an accuracy of 0.6 degrees and a precision of 0.03 degrees.

It is also equipped with a scene camera, which records the driver's first-person view, providing a 106-degree diagonal field of view with a resolution of 1920 x 1080 gaze-overlapped video for post-processing.
This study utilised a 2 x 2 within-participants design.
The two main independent variables included were: level of automation (manual driving and hands-off L2 assisted driving) and lighting of the driving environment (daytime and after dark).
Participants completed four experimental drives, presented in a counterbalanced order, with a 5-minute break after every two drives.

For the manual driving conditions, participants were told that they had full control of the movement of the car, and they were instructed to follow the traffic rules as they would when they were driving in a real urban setting with a speed limit of 30 mph.
Participants drove along a two-lane urban roadway, with cars travelling in the oncoming lane at the rate of one car per kilometre.
The urban environment was populated with ambient road users and static road elements, spaced equally every 40 metres and positioned randomly to the left and right of the driver.

These included individually walking pedestrians approaching the roadway from the roadside, groups of talking pedestrians, standing cyclists, parked trucks, parked cars, bus stops (see Figure 2 for examples).
text.formatted: These included individually walking pedestrians approaching the roadway from the roadside, groups of talking pedestrians, standing cyclists, parked trucks, parked cars, bus stops (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref> for examples).

text.text: These were positioned in equal proportions to the left and right, to avoid any biased visual attention allocation and scanning patterns to one location.

For every drive, participants also encountered six actual or potential (materialised or non-materialised, respectively) hazardous events, including pedestrian crossing the road and oncoming vehicle turning across the path of the ego vehicle, some of which required resumption of manual control in the hands-off L2 conditions, to avoid a collision.
However, the eye tracking and vehicle data associated with these events are reported in another manuscript (Lee et al., 2026).
text.formatted: However, the eye tracking and vehicle data associated with these events are reported in another manuscript <ref type="bibr">(Lee et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: For the L2 assisted driving conditions (SAE, 2021), the car was equipped with a driving assistance system that was capable of maintaining the vehicle within the driving lane and adhering to the speed limit (30mph).
During these conditions, participants were first exposed to one minute of manual driving before the system became available.

When the system first became available, an auditory message "Automation Available" was presented, and participants were instructed to engage with the system as soon as possible by pressing a specified button on the steering wheel.
Once the system was engaged, drivers were asked to have their hands off the steering wheel and their foot off the pedals.
However, the system was not be able to detect or respond to any hazardous events.

For this reason, participants were required to monitor the road environment at all times and take over manual control if necessary by pressing the specified buttons on the steering wheel or turning the steering wheel for more than 2 degrees or pressing the brake pedal.

If they resumed manual control to deal with a materialised or non-materialised hazardous event, they were told to re-engage the system as soon as possible, or the system would automatically re-engage after 10 seconds.
All hazardous events were resolved within this 10-second window.
The status of the driving assistance system was displayed on the Human Machine Interface (HMI) located in the dashboard area (see
Upon arrival, participants were briefed on the experimental procedure and allowed to ask any questions they might have regarding the experiment before providing their consent.

Participants completed a series of self-report measures to provide their trust and perceived safety towards automated vehicles prior to the experimental drives (data are not reported in this manuscript).

They then took part in two practice drives (manual driving in after dark and L2 assisted driving in daytime environments) to familiarise themselves with the operational controls of the driving simulator.
Participants were accompanied by the experimenter during these drives.
After the practice drives, calibration of the eye tracker was conducted, which was then repeated before every experimental drive.
Participants completed four experimental drives on their own, each of which lasted approximately 9 minutes.

Once all experimental drives were completed, participants were once again asked to complete a series of self-report measures to report their perceived driving skills, difficulties associated with driving after dark and their trust and perceived safety towards automated vehicles (data are not reported in this manuscript).
Participants were then debriefed and compensated £30 for their time.
Based on the urban driving context, five main AOIs were specified: Forward Roadway, Left Periphery, Rear View Mirror, Right Periphery, and Instrument Cluster (see Figure 4).
text.formatted: Based on the urban driving context, five main AOIs were specified: Forward Roadway, Left Periphery, Rear View Mirror, Right Periphery, and Instrument Cluster (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">4</ref>).

text.text: Forward Roadway covered the immediate forward roadway region from the driver's perspective, whereas the Instrument Cluster covered the speedometer and the HMI.
The left periphery covered the regions within the leftward field of view from the driver's perspective, such as potential hazards on the left pavement, and the left-hand mirror.
In contrast, the right periphery covered the regions within the rightward field of view from the driver's perspective, such as potential hazards on the right pavement, and the right-hand mirror.
Gaze points that were not mapped onto these five main AOIs were classified as "Others", which included the sky and incabin areas.

Four AOIs were considered for further analysis, with the "Rear View Mirror" and "Others" AOIs being exempted as drivers rarely glanced at these AOIs (on average, 0.91 % and 0.35 %, respectively across four experimental drives).

Fixations were identified using the in-built Velocity-Threshold Identification Gaze Filter (I-VT filter) algorithm within Tobii Pro Lab, with a threshold of 100 degrees/second (Salvucci & Goldberg, 2000).
text.formatted: Fixations were identified using the in-built Velocity-Threshold Identification Gaze Filter (I-VT filter) algorithm within Tobii Pro Lab, with a threshold of 100 degrees/second <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Salvucci & Goldberg, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Fixations with a minimum threshold of 100 milliseconds were filtered, which is consistent with previous studies with head-mounted eye trackers (Konstantopoulos et al., 2010; Urwyler et al., 2015).

text.text: Glance-derived dependent variables were then constructed for each AOI to answer the research questions.

A glance is defined as a sequence of consecutive fixations within the boundary of the same AOI, including all intervals in between (ISO, 2020; Morando et al., 2021; Qin et al., 2025; Seppelt et al., 2017).
text.formatted: A glance is defined as a sequence of consecutive fixations within the boundary of the same AOI, including all intervals in between (ISO, 2020; <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Morando et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Qin et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Seppelt et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Dependent variables considered in this study were the horizontal and vertical gaze dispersion, and percentage of glance time towards each AOI.

Horizontal and vertical gaze dispersion were used to capture the spread of drivers' visual scanning patterns across the driving scene and were computed using the standard deviation of Gaze Point X and Gaze Point Y coordinates, respectively (Goncalves et al., 2020; Louw & Merat, 2017), in pixels.
text.formatted: Horizontal and vertical gaze dispersion were used to capture the spread of drivers' visual scanning patterns across the driving scene and were computed using the standard deviation of Gaze Point X and Gaze Point Y coordinates, respectively <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Goncalves et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Louw & Merat, 2017)</ref>, in pixels.

text.text: To capture how drivers distributed their overall visual attention across specific areas of the driving environment, percentage of glance time spent towards each AOI was calculated as the proportion of time spent glancing at each AOI relative to the total driving duration for the selected road segments (see Section 2.7.3), expressed as a percentage.

To understand how drivers allocate their visual attention in an urban environment across different lighting conditions of the driving environment (daytime, after dark) and levels of automation (manual driving, hands-off L2 assisted driving), road segments containing oncoming cars and other ambient traffic were selected for analysis (see Section 2.4 for more details on the ambient traffic present).
Only straight road segments were included to prevent the influence of road curvature on gaze behaviour.

In addition, data from the road segments 100 metres before and 100 metres after each materialised and non-materialised hazardous event were excluded, to prevent drivers' reaction to those events from influencing the gaze behaviour (data associated with these hazardous events is reported in Lee et al., 2026).
To answer the research questions, data were analysed using mixed-effects models (Stroup, 2012).
text.formatted: To answer the research questions, data were analysed using mixed-effects models <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Stroup, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: All analyses were conducted using RStudio version 2025.5.0.496 (Rstudio Team, 2025).
Model estimation was performed with the lmer and glmmTMB packages, and calculation of estimated marginal means (EMMs) and post-hoc comparisons were obtained through the emmeans package.

text.text: To account for potential order and learning effects, the run number (coded as 1 to 4) and the two-way interaction between run number and the independent variables were also considered.
Participant ID was included as a random factor to account for individual differences.

A backward elimination method (James et al., 2021) was employed to refine the model by assessing its Akaike Information Criterions (AIC) values and the Likelihood Ratio Test (LRT) to reduce the probability of overfitting and maintaining the model's parsimony.
With this approach, a full model that consisted of all fixed effect factors mentioned in the previous paragraph was first considered.

Factors associated with run number were eliminated one at a time if they did not contribute significantly to model fit, while retaining the key variables of the experiment, as they were not the primary factor of the experiment.
The model assumptions of the final fitted model were first evaluated prior to interpretation.
Normality of residuals was evaluated by inspecting the Q-Q plot and assessed by the Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test (Venables & Ripley, 2002).
text.formatted: Normality of residuals was evaluated by inspecting the Q-Q plot and assessed by the Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Venables & Ripley, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Homoscedasticity was examined via residuals against fitted value plots.
For dependent variables where the assumptions were met, the analysis proceeded with the Linear Mixed Model (LMM; Stroup, 2012).

text.text: Out of 176 potential data points (44 participants x 4 experimental drives), some were excluded due to technical issues associated with the driving simulator or eye tracker, or because participants failed to follow the experimental protocol.
The final analyses included 164 data points: 39 for hands-off L2 assisted driving in daytime and after dark conditions, and 43 for manual driving in daytime and after dark conditions.

To answer the second research question, regarding visual attention to different types of ambient traffic, two categories of ambient road elements were operationalised, based on the distinction proposed by Crundall et al. (2012): (1) the "Behavioural Prediction" (BP) element, which included the walking pedestrians and cyclist; and (2) the "Inanimate Object" (IO), which included the parked cars and trucks, which were static elements that could potentially occlude other road users from the driver's view.

(2012)</ref>: (1) the "Behavioural Prediction" (BP) element, which included the walking pedestrians and cyclist; and (2) the "Inanimate Object" (IO), which included the parked cars and trucks, which were static elements that could potentially occlude other road users from the driver's view.

text.text: Given that no hazard emerged from behind the static elements in the present study, this category was termed differently from Crundall et al.'s (2012) "Environmental Prediction" (EP) element.

text.text: GLMMs were constructed to investigate whether these different elements elicited distinct attention allocation patterns across the various experimental drives.
The dependent variable for these models was the mean glance duration towards the left and right peripheries to capture the amount of visual attention devoted to these areas of the driving scene.
Rather than analysing the entire drive, this analysis focused exclusively on segments where either BP or IO elements were presented within those specified AOIs.

The models were refined using a backward elimination process, where the three-way interaction was then excluded as it did not significantly improve the model fit (see Table 1 for the final retained fixed effects).

text.text: As shown in Figure 5, the contour plots in L2 assisted driving panels showed a more concentrated vertical gaze pattern relative to that observed in manual driving conditions.

In contrast, the marginal histogram for Gaze Point Y during L2 assisted driving after dark condition showed a distinct secondary peak, reflecting greater variability in vertical gaze locations.
The main effect of level of automation on horizontal gaze dispersion was not found to be significant (F (1, 115.39) = 2.380, p = .126).

text.text: Based on the model predictions, vertical gaze dispersion was significantly reduced by 33.4% in L2 assisted driving (EMMs = 69.2 pixels, SE = 2.92) relative to manual driving conditions (EMMs = 103.9 pixels, SE = 2.87).
Both horizontal (F (1, 114.92) = 0.391, p =.533) and vertical gaze dispersion (F (1, 118.24) = 0.339, p = .562) were found to be similar across daytime and after dark driving environments.
No significant interactions were found for horizontal gaze dispersion (F (1, 114.92) = 0.145, p =.704).
In contrast, a significant interaction was found between level of automation and lighting conditions for vertical gaze dispersion (F (1, 118.24) = 4.722, p = .032).

To examine whether drivers allocated different levels of visual attention to Behavioural Prediction (BP) and Inanimate Object (IO) elements across experimental conditions, mean glance durations towards the left and right peripheral environments were analysed when these elements were present.

Results showed that drivers allocated greater visual attention to BP elements than IO for both the left (z = 3.86, p < .001; see Figure 10) and right (z = 2.89, p = .004; see Figure 11) peripheral environments.
text.formatted: Results showed that drivers allocated greater visual attention to BP elements than IO for both the left (z = 3.86, p < .001; see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_12">10</ref>) and right (z = 2.89, p = .004; see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_13">11</ref>) peripheral environments.

text.text: For the left periphery, BP elements elicited significantly longer mean glance durations (EMMs = 845.95, SE = 41.51) than IO (EMMs = 685.66, SE = 34.78).

This greater visual attention allocation towards BP elements at the left periphery was consistent across experimental conditions with no significant interactions seen between element type and lighting condition, or element type and level of automation.
For the right periphery, however, the difference in mean glance duration between BP and IO was moderated by lighting conditions (z = -1.97, p = .049).

Post-hoc Bonferronicorrected comparisons showed that the BP elements elicited significantly longer mean glance durations than IO, only during daytime conditions (z = 3.39, p = .004), with no significant differences found after dark (p = 1.000).
No significant interaction was found between level of automation and element type.
This driving simulator study explored the effects of lighting conditions in the driving environment and levels of automation on drivers' visual attention allocation and scanning patterns.

The study also investigated whether visual attention allocation towards different types of ambient traffic present in an urban environment (i.e., BP and IO) differed between manual driving and L2 assisted driving, for these different driving environments.
Contrary to previous findings (Louw & Merat, 2017; Mackenzie & Harris, 2015), our results showed that drivers had similar horizontal gaze dispersion patterns in manual and L2 assisted driving.
text.formatted: Contrary to previous findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Louw & Merat, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Mackenzie & Harris, 2015)</ref>, our results showed that drivers had similar horizontal gaze dispersion patterns in manual and L2 assisted driving.

text.text: This difference in findings from previous studies could be due to the urban traffic environment used in the present study, compared to use of car following tasks in a motorway scenario for previous studies.

The regular presence of ambient urban traffic located in the peripheral areas may have consistently attracted drivers' visual attention, potentially resulting in high horizontal gaze dispersion, regardless of level of driving automation, with the motorway studies having comparatively less objects of interest in the peripheral areas, coupled with the need to focus on the lead vehicle, in case of an impending collision.

Although horizontal gaze dispersion did not differ between the two levels of automation, results from the percentage of glance time towards each AOI showed that drivers spent more time monitoring the left and right peripheral environments throughout the drive during L2 assisted driving, when compared to manual driving.

This suggests that L2 assisted driving did not alter the overall horizontal extent of visual scanning, but it did increase the amount of time drivers spent monitoring both left and right peripheral regions of the driving environment throughout the drive.

The reduced operational demand offered by hands-off L2 driving is thought to reduce workload, providing more resources for drivers to monitor their surroundings (De Winter et al., 2014; Mackenzie & Harris, 2015).
text.formatted: The reduced operational demand offered by hands-off L2 driving is thought to reduce workload, providing more resources for drivers to monitor their surroundings <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(De Winter et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Mackenzie & Harris, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Participants' visual attention allocation also evolved across runs, likely reflecting how they adapted to the driving environment.

Participants initially devoted more attention to the left peripheral environment, as reflected by a higher percentage of glance time towards the left periphery, where potential hazards were closer to the ego vehicle, before increasing attention towards the right periphery in the later runs.

This shift was accompanied by a reduction in horizontal gaze dispersion across runs, which suggests that drivers initially adopted a broader exploratory scanning strategy, and subsequently adapted their visual sampling behaviour as they became familiar with the driving environment.
Drivers' visual attention towards different types of ambient urban traffic within the peripheral environment varied, based on their nature.

Regardless of level of automation, drivers spent more time looking at Behavioural Prediction elements (e.g., walking pedestrians and cyclists) relative to Inanimate Objects (e.g., parked trucks and parked cars).
This finding aligns with Crundall et al. (2012) who found that BP stimuli attract more attention compared to static elements.
text.formatted: This finding aligns with <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Crundall et al. (2012)</ref> who found that BP stimuli attract more attention compared to static elements.

text.text: This pattern may reflect the dynamic nature of the BP stimuli, which are more likely to trigger bottom-up attention mechanisms.
In addition, pedestrians and cyclists pose a greater potential collision risk than parked vehicles, as they may be perceived as more likely to enter the roadway.

This bias appeared to be robust across automation levels, suggesting that drivers continued to focus more on safety-relevant road users, as an attempt to anticipate potential hazards and maintain situation awareness.

Consistent with previous studies (Goncalves et al., 2020; Morando et al., 2019; Morando et al., 2020; Pipkorn et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2025). the vertical gaze dispersion seen during uninterrupted driving in hands-off L2 conditions was significantly lower than that observed for manual driving.
text.formatted: Consistent with previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Goncalves et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Morando et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Morando et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Pipkorn et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Qin et al., 2025)</ref>. the vertical gaze dispersion seen during uninterrupted driving in hands-off L2 conditions was significantly lower than that observed for manual driving.

text.text: This is because during manual driving, drivers are responsible for the moment-to-moment control of the vehicle, and visuomotor coordination remains intact (Mole et al., 2019).
text.formatted: This is because during manual driving, drivers are responsible for the moment-to-moment control of the vehicle, and visuomotor coordination remains intact <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Mole et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: They are therefore required to acquire information from the forward roadway and instrument cluster to guide the car's trajectory and maintain its speed.

This interpretation is also supported by the percentage of glance time data to each AOI, which showed that drivers had a lower percentage of glance time towards the instrument cluster and forward roadway during L2 assisted driving, compared to manual driving.

In terms of the effect of lighting on visual scanning patterns, the percentage of glance time towards the four AOIs and the horizontal and vertical gaze dispersion patterns were found to be similar for the daytime and after dark conditions.
These results are consistent with those reported in a previous driving simulator study (Konstantopoulos et al., 2010).
text.formatted: These results are consistent with those reported in a previous driving simulator study <ref type="bibr">(Konstantopoulos et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: However, the lighting conditions of the driving environment in this study was found to moderate visual attention allocation on the different urban elements, shown in mean glance duration towards the AOIs when these elements were presented.
Specifically, the greater visual attention allocation towards the BP elements, when compared to IOs, was only observed in daytime, especially for those items located in the right periphery.

The absence of this difference in after dark may reflect a reduced ability to distinguish between BP and IO under reduced visibility, consistent with previous arguments that reduced saliency of environmental cues in after dark environments hinders drivers' ability to perceive and interpret road information (Wood, 2020).
text.formatted: The absence of this difference in after dark may reflect a reduced ability to distinguish between BP and IO under reduced visibility, consistent with previous arguments that reduced saliency of environmental cues in after dark environments hinders drivers' ability to perceive and interpret road information <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Wood, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This effect appeared to be particularly pronounced in the right periphery, potentially because the ego vehicle's headlamps primarily illuminated the forward roadway, and, to some extent, the left periphery, creating lower levels of luminance in the right peripheral space.

Consequently, drivers may have found it more difficult to distinguish between BP and IO elements in the right periphery, resulting in a non-significant difference in mean glance duration across the two element types in after dark.
L2 assisted driving reduced vertical gaze dispersion compared to manual driving; however, this reduction was less pronounced in the after dark lighting conditions.

This pattern may be attributable to the reduced visibility of the after dark environment, which limits drivers' capability for detecting any ambient urban traffic in the far distance (Garay et al., 2004; Garay-Vega et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This pattern may be attributable to the reduced visibility of the after dark environment, which limits drivers' capability for detecting any ambient urban traffic in the far distance <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Garay et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Garay-Vega et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lee et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, ambient traffic only became visible at a closer distance in the after dark environment.

As objects closer to the ego vehicle are projected lower in the visual field relative to the horizon line, drivers would be required to allocate their gaze across a broader range of vertical locations when monitoring the road environment, resulting in greater vertical gaze dispersion.

Consequently, although L2 assisted driving reduced the necessity for downward gaze shifts towards the instrument cluster for speed-control purposes, drivers still needed to vertically distribute their gaze to sample the nearby roadway environment.

This interpretation is consistent with the distinct secondary peak observed in the Gaze Point Y distribution during L2 assisted driving after dark, indicating greater variability in vertical gaze locations.

Overall, these findings suggest that the effect of L2 assisted driving on visual scanning is not uniform across lighting conditions, with drivers appearing to adapt their visual scanning behaviours to meet the increased demands of reduced visibility after dark.
Future design of driving assistance system may be benefit from incorporating night-vision camera system to support better visual attention in reduced visibility environment.

One main shortcoming of this study is the use of a driving simulator to explore visual scanning patterns when driving after dark, which might not provide the same levels of luminance associated with driving at night in the real world (Wood & Chaparro, 2011).
text.formatted: One main shortcoming of this study is the use of a driving simulator to explore visual scanning patterns when driving after dark, which might not provide the same levels of luminance associated with driving at night in the real world <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Wood & Chaparro, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Also, for practical reasons, participants took part in this driving simulator study during daytime hours, which limits our understanding of how circadian rhythms may have affected driver fatigue and influenced performance.

Therefore, further research is warranted to investigate how nighttime driving affects drivers' visual attention and scan patterns in a real-world urban environment, and how this is influenced by levels of automation, to improve ecological validity and a more holistic understanding of this topic.
